claims.evidence: Mark moves from the synagogue to Simon and Andrew’s house, then describes a crowd at the door. Capernaum’s excavated basalt dwellings give material context for a village household.
claims.interpretation: Kinship, care and hospitality belong in the setting of Jesus’ ministry. Mark’s crowded doorway is more useful here than imagining a modern private living room.
claims.limit: A surviving house cannot establish its owner’s name. This drawing does not identify Peter’s house or reproduce the roof opened in Mark 2.

claims.evidence: Mark names fishers, a boat and hired workers. Fiensy’s review of Galilean pottery research describes vessels circulating beyond their production villages.
claims.interpretation: Farming, fishing and crafts connected households to wider exchange. A village was not necessarily economically isolated; neither does a market connection prove that everyone prospered.
claims.limit: Scholars disagree about exploitation and living standards. No standard household budget, tax percentage or class label for every fisher can be recovered from these examples.

claims.evidence: The Capernaum excavation account describes courtyard houses, grain-grinding implements and ovens for bread. These remains span phases; they provide context for household work rather than identifying a particular Gospel household.
claims.interpretation: Preparing food, maintaining a house and caring for people take labour. A grinding tool can suggest an activity; it cannot by itself tell us the worker’s gender or legal status.
claims.limit: The courtyard is schematic. A recovered tool is not a biography, and a house plan cannot assign a fixed task to every person. No named household is identified here.

claims.evidence: Mark 2 places Levi at a tax office after Jesus goes out beside the sea. Luke 3 distinguishes Antipas’s Galilee from Pilate’s Judaea.
claims.interpretation: Exchange and government enter the same local story. Regional offices matter even when the scene begins with ordinary work.
claims.limit: These texts do not supply a uniform tax rate, a recovered toll building or a complete household budget.

claims.evidence: Luke depicts Sabbath reading at Nazareth. At Migdal, excavators found benches and a carved stone bearing a menorah. A coin dated 43 CE lay beneath the final reading-room mosaic.
claims.interpretation: Reading and teaching were local communal activities. The carving may evoke the Temple, but its full meaning and the stone’s function are interpretations.
claims.limit: Migdal’s final floor should not be pictured as the floor Jesus stood on. Capernaum’s prominent white synagogue is centuries later. These are different buildings and phases.

claims.evidence: The Migdal excavation report describes a stone bearing a seven-branched menorah. Its placement and carved imagery are material evidence.
claims.interpretation: The image invites comparison with Temple imagery. A proposed table function or interpretation of every motif adds an argument to what was excavated.
claims.limit: The carving does not preserve an order of worship, establish Jesus’ attendance or settle how every synagogue was organised.

claims.evidence: The Jerusalem dedication of Theodotos names Torah reading and teaching. Acts 13 depicts reading from the Law and Prophets at Pisidian Antioch, followed by an invitation to speak.
claims.interpretation: Language, leadership and practice could vary across communities. Acts 23 also portrays disagreement about resurrection; Pharisees and Sadducees do not exhaust the diversity of Jewish life.
claims.limit: Theodotos’s inscription was not found at Migdal. Acts narrates particular assemblies; neither source supplies a universal synagogue liturgy.

claims.evidence: Deuteronomy prescribes pilgrimage festivals; John places Jesus at the Temple during Booths. A surviving Greek warning inscription forbids outsiders to cross an inner sanctuary boundary, threatening death.
claims.interpretation: Pilgrimage connected worship with movement and practical needs. Acts 21 makes a boundary accusation central to the confrontation over Paul; the narrator calls it a supposition.
claims.limit: The inscription does not prove that Paul brought Trophimus inside. A festival command is not an attendance count, and an inner boundary is not the whole Temple complex.

claims.evidence: The Greek dedication of Theodotos, a priest and synagogue leader, records provision for Torah reading, instruction and lodging for people from abroad. It is commonly dated before 70 CE.
claims.interpretation: Temple and synagogue should not be treated as successive institutions, one simply replacing the other. Visitors could encounter teaching, hospitality and Temple worship in the same city.
claims.limit: The dating is scholarly, not a date written on the stone. One dedication does not tell us every synagogue’s practices, and it is not securely identified with a synagogue in Acts.

claims.evidence: John 4 depicts a Samaritan woman contrasting her community’s mountain with Jerusalem. Luke 9 describes a Samaritan village refusing travellers because they are going to Jerusalem.
claims.interpretation: Samaritans were a distinct community, with a different sacred centre. Within Jewish communities too, Acts depicts disagreement over resurrection; Luke even shows some Pharisees warning Jesus of danger.
claims.limit: These are particular literary depictions. They do not prove that every Jewish traveller avoided Samaria, or that every Pharisee had the same attitude toward Jesus.

claims.evidence: Excavations of wealthy Upper City residences revealed plastered, stepped pools interpreted as ritual baths, alongside decorated rooms and courtyards.
claims.interpretation: Purity practices had a material setting within household life. Compare the practical needs of a festival journey in Luke 2 with the Temple’s economic and religious setting in Mark 11.
claims.limit: These residences are not a representative sample of every Jerusalem household. The pool drawing is not a surveyed bath or the route required of every pilgrim.

claims.evidence: The damaged Latin dedication names Pontius Pilate as prefect of Judaea. The Israel Museum records its discovery reused in Caesarea’s theatre staircase.
claims.interpretation: An object’s findspot can differ from its original display. An official Latin text also does not establish the language or religion of every resident.
claims.limit: Restored letters must not be treated as surviving ones. The stone does not identify the location of Jesus’ trial or provide the original building’s complete form.

claims.evidence: Acts 24 presents accusations and Paul’s defence before Felix, followed by continuing custody. Acts 25 names Festus as his successor. Acts 10 separately introduces Cornelius in a military household.
claims.interpretation: Governors, military officers, accusers and prisoners occupy different positions. Caesarea’s place in these stories cannot be reduced to a single episode under Pilate.
claims.limit: Acts supplies the narrative, not a transcript. No chair, prison or courtroom in the illustration is identified as Paul’s.

claims.evidence: Acts 27 distinguishes soldiers, prisoners and companions. It names an initial vessel from Adramyttium, followed by a change to an Alexandrian ship at Myra.
claims.interpretation: Military custody and commercial transport meet at the port. An official, prisoner and free traveller do not have interchangeable freedom of movement.
claims.limit: This is a selected narrative itinerary. It does not document every passenger’s contract or establish a regular scheduled service.

claims.evidence: In 1 Corinthians 11, Paul rebukes divisions at the gathering: one person is hungry while another is drunk. He asks why they shame those who have little.
claims.interpretation: Sharing a religious identity did not automatically dissolve economic difference. The text allows us to see a conflict in a particular assembly, rather than imagine every early gathering as socially equal.
claims.limit: Paul does not provide a guest list or a plan of the building. “Rich in the dining room, poor in the courtyard” is a reconstruction, not a sentence in his letter.

claims.evidence: The letters explicitly name assemblies in houses. Philemon addresses a house assembly and speaks of Onesimus as a slave and a beloved brother; 1 Corinthians also addresses enslaved people.
claims.interpretation: A household could contain unequal legal and social positions. A large house, a workshop or restricted dining space may help us imagine possibilities; no one plan explains all communities.
claims.limit: The dashed rooms are hypothetical. Slavery was coercive ownership, not simply employment. Philemon’s appeal does not document Onesimus’s eventual legal status.

claims.evidence: Paul’s instruction in 1 Corinthians 11:33 is to wait for one another when they gather to eat. Romans 16 names Prisca and Aquila’s house assembly and commends Phoebe from Cenchreae.
claims.interpretation: The response concerns how people treat one another. Women appear among the named people sustaining these networks, not merely as anonymous background figures.
claims.limit: The inclusive diagram illustrates the instruction, not proof that the Corinthians obeyed. Phoebe, Prisca and Aquila must not be placed at this imagined table as an attested guest list.

claims.evidence: Acts 18 connects Paul, Aquila and Priscilla through a shared craft. First Corinthians 9 argues about the right to material support; 12:13 names enslaved and free people within the body.
claims.interpretation: Income, hospitality and dependence were negotiated within these communities. The assembly’s meals belong alongside its working lives.
claims.limit: Neither text supplies a standard apostolic income or an excavated workshop address. A public platform at Corinth is a plausible civic setting for Acts 18, not proof of the exact place of the hearing.

claims.evidence: Paul allows eating what is sold in the meat market without investigating it for conscience’s sake (1 Corinthians 10:25–26). His earlier discussion also attends to people affected by associations with idols.
claims.interpretation: Do not flatten an entire urban food economy into a single religious action. A purchaser’s situation differs from participation at a cult table.
claims.limit: The passage does not say that all meat came from temples. The drawn counter is an analogy, not an identified shop used by Paul.

claims.evidence: Paul permits accepting an unbeliever’s invitation and eating without inquiry. If someone points out that food was offered in sacrifice, he advises abstaining for that person’s sake.
claims.interpretation: The social meaning of the act changes with the situation. Conscience and the effect on another person matter alongside the origin of the food.
claims.limit: This is Paul’s instruction to Corinth, not a universal Roman etiquette code. Romans 14 shows that food and the observance of days also divided the Roman assemblies.

claims.evidence: In 1 Corinthians 10:20–21 Paul rejects participation in sacrificial worship. At Pompeii, the food shop of Vetutius Placidus preserves a counter, a household shrine and an adjoining dwelling.
claims.interpretation: The Italian example makes the proximity of commerce, home and worship tangible. Paul draws a boundary around cult participation even while permitting ordinary market purchases.
claims.limit: Pompeii is neither Corinth nor proof of a Christian gathering. Roman society contained diverse local cults and communities; a shrine in one shop does not establish everyone’s beliefs.

claims.evidence: Rathmayr’s research abstract dates the beginning of Terrace House 2, Unit 7 to the early first century CE and describes later rebuilding. First Corinthians 16 connects Ephesus with greetings from Aquila and Prisca’s house assembly.
claims.interpretation: An elite house helps us ask about space and status. It cannot stand for all residents; its later appearance cannot simply be carried back to Paul’s lifetime.
claims.limit: The house is not identified as Aquila and Prisca’s. The research abstract was reviewed, not the complete excavation volume.

claims.evidence: Acts 19:23–27 connects silver-shrine manufacture with concern about artisans’ income and the honour of Artemis.
claims.interpretation: The narrative joins economic interest to religious commitment. That overlap differs from Corinth’s question about purchasing meat or accepting a dinner invitation.
claims.limit: This is a particular conflict in Acts, not evidence that every craft worker opposed Christians or every purchase was a religious act.

claims.evidence: Acts describes a gathering in the theatre with people shouting different things. The town clerk appeals to courts, proconsuls and a lawful assembly.
claims.interpretation: Local civic institutions operated within provincial government. A crowd, its organisers and an official can have different motives even in the same scene.
claims.limit: The narrative is not a transcript of civic proceedings. Visible monuments may include later building phases; no complete first-century theatre is reconstructed here.

claims.evidence: Acts describes slow progress against the wind, shelter along Crete and a debate about wintering. Later, an Alexandrian ship that had wintered at Malta carries the party onward.
claims.interpretation: Weather and waiting shape the narrative. The route is not a timetable, and a favourable breeze in one moment does not guarantee safe passage.
claims.limit: This is a reading of Acts, not a weather reconstruction. Stanford’s ORBIS explores mode and season around 200 CE; its model should not silently become first-century travel data.

claims.evidence: At Myra, a centurion puts the party aboard an Alexandrian ship. When Paul warns about continuing, the centurion listens to the ship’s master and owner instead.
claims.interpretation: The story combines military custody with commercial expertise. Elsewhere Acts shows Roman citizenship affecting Paul’s treatment at Philippi: status changes what a person can claim.
claims.limit: These are narrated decisions, not a universal shipping regulation. A prisoner, a shipowner and a free passenger do not have interchangeable freedom of movement.

claims.evidence: The ship in Acts 27 carries wheat that is thrown overboard. After Malta, Acts names Syracuse, Rhegium and Puteoli; believers offer hospitality, and others come out from Rome to meet Paul.
claims.interpretation: Transport of goods, military movement and community hospitality intersect. Romans 16’s commendation of Phoebe similarly shows a network of people expected to receive and assist a traveller.
claims.limit: Phoebe’s exact itinerary is not given. This diagram follows Acts’s selected stops; it is not her route or a composite of all Paul’s voyages.

claims.evidence: The French Ministry of Culture describes the excavated hull and wine amphorae of Madrague de Giens, wrecked off southern Gaul around 75–60 BCE. Acts 27:38 separately describes wheat being discarded.
claims.interpretation: A wreck provides material evidence of maritime freight. Paul’s own recollection of shipwrecks in 2 Corinthians adds another literary perspective on vulnerability at sea.
claims.limit: Different dates, cargoes and routes: this earlier western wreck is not Paul’s ship. The restored mast and sail are schematic; no ship capacity or journey time is calculated.

teachingSequence.title: A small place. A connected life.
teachingSequence.connection: Move from household work to an assembly at nearby Migdal. These are connected settings, not one excavated settlement.

teachingSequence.title: Shared Scripture. Different local settings.
teachingSequence.connection: Local reading and teaching coexisted with pilgrimage and Temple worship. Continue to Jerusalem.

teachingSequence.title: One destination. Different ways of belonging.
teachingSequence.connection: Move west to Caesarea, then forward several decades: Pilate’s dedication and Paul’s hearings belong to different administrations.

teachingSequence.title: One port. Different kinds of power.
teachingSequence.connection: Across the Mediterranean, livelihood and legal status also shape the gatherings addressed by Paul. Continue to Corinth.

teachingSequence.title: At one gathering. Not on equal terms.
teachingSequence.connection: The meal begins before anyone arrives: food is bought, invitations accepted, and social obligations negotiated on the city street.

teachingSequence.title: The same food. A different situation.
teachingSequence.connection: Cross to Ephesus, where Acts describes another interaction between craft, religious honour and civic authority. Similar pressures do not make the cities identical.

teachingSequence.title: A city does not speak with one voice.
teachingSequence.connection: People and letters connect these cities. End by returning to the hazards, cargoes and hospitality of travel toward Rome.

teachingSequence.title: A route is more than a line.
teachingSequence.connection: Return to the passages with a sharper question: which features belong to this place, this date and these people?
